questions.q: What does a hypervisor do for a virtual machine?
options: It compiles the application's code
It emulates a complete computer, letting each VM run its own full guest operating system
It shares one kernel across every VM on the host
It replaces the need for an operating system entirely
questions.explain: A hypervisor emulates hardware so each virtual machine can boot and run its own complete guest OS, including its own kernel.

questions.q: What is the key architectural difference between a container and a virtual machine?
options: Containers run on bare metal with no host OS at all
A container shares the host's single kernel, while a VM boots its own separate guest kernel
A VM shares the host's kernel, while a container boots its own kernel
There is no architectural difference -- the terms are interchangeable
questions.explain: Containers virtualize at the OS level and share the host kernel; VMs virtualize a full computer via a hypervisor and each run their own guest kernel.

questions.q: Why do containers typically start in under a second while VMs take minutes?
options: Containers use faster hard drives than VMs
Containers skip booting a guest operating system entirely, since they share the host's kernel
VMs are always run on slower cloud providers
Containers don't actually run any processes until requested
questions.explain: Because a container has no guest kernel to boot, startup only involves starting the application process -- not an entire operating system.

questions.q: Why does Northbridge Retail run its container hosts on top of virtual machines rather than choosing only one or the other?
options: Because containers cannot run in the cloud without a VM
Because the VM provides a strong security boundary around the whole host, while containers give fast, efficient packaging for individual services inside it
Because VMs are required to install Docker
Because running both is purely a licensing requirement
questions.explain: VMs and containers solve different problems and are commonly layered together: the VM isolates the host machine, and containers isolate and package the applications running on it.

questions.q: Which of these is generally true when comparing container density to VM density on the same host?
options: A host can usually run far more containers than VMs, since each container only consumes what its app needs rather than a full OS
VMs and containers always have identical density on any host
A host can only ever run one container or one VM at a time
VMs always achieve higher density than containers
questions.explain: Because containers don't carry the overhead of a full guest OS, a single host can typically run far more containers than virtual machines.
